malrules.name: Ignore-Decimal-Point
malrules.description: Students ignore the decimal point and treat decimal numbers as whole numbers, applying whole number arithmetic procedures without regard to place value. This error stems from students computing by relying solely on syntax-based rules where semantic knowledge has no effect on performance (Hiebert & Wearne, 1985).

malrules.name: Longer-Is-Larger
malrules.description: When comparing decimal numbers, students incorrectly believe that more decimal digits means a larger number. For example, they think 0.45 is larger than 0.8 because 0.45 has more digits. This stems from overgeneralizing whole number comparison rules to decimals, a phenomenon extensively documented by Steinle & Stacey (1998, 2004) as one of the most prevalent decimal misconceptions.

malrules.name: Right-Align-Decimals
malrules.description: Students align decimal numbers by the rightmost digit instead of by the decimal point when performing addition or subtraction. This error stems from overgeneralizing whole number alignment procedures where right-alignment is correct. Hiebert & Wearne (1985) found that students compute by relying on syntax-based rules without semantic understanding of place value.

malrules.name: Shorter-Is-Larger
malrules.description: Students incorrectly believe that decimals with fewer decimal places are larger. For example, they think 0.3 is larger than 0.496. This misconception is linked to denominator-focused thinking, reciprocal thinking, or fraction knowledge interference (Steinle & Stacey, 1998; Resnick et al., 1989).

malrules.name: Whole-Number-Thinking
malrules.description: Students incorrectly treat decimals as if they demonstrate the properties of whole numbers. This fundamental misconception, termed the 'Whole Number rule' by Resnick et al. (1989), leads to errors such as thinking 0.25 is greater than 0.7 because 25 > 7, or computing 3.7 + 2.5 = 62 by treating the numbers as 37 + 25.
